subject: Cognitive Science
title: Updating Your Priors
description: A micro-lesson that makes Updating Your Priors usable.

hook.text: You're 90% sure it won't rain. Then you see dark clouds. Do you stubbornly keep your estimate? Of course not.

buildup.text: Bayesian updating means adjusting your beliefs proportionally when new evidence arrives.

discovery.text: Strong prior evidence requires strong new evidence to shift. Weak priors should shift more easily.

twist.text: Most people anchor too hard on their initial belief. New data should change your mind more than it does.

climax.text: Good thinkers hold probabilities, not certainties. They're always updating, never locked in.

punchline.text: Change your mind when the evidence changes.

quiz.question: What is Bayesian updating?
options: Adjusting beliefs proportionally to new evidence

details.summary: Bayesian updating means adjusting your beliefs proportionally to the strength of new evidence. Start with a prior belief, encounter evidence, and update toward whatever the evidence supports. Good thinkers update continuously rather than clinging to initial positions.
details.whyItMatters: Rigid beliefs in a changing world are a liability. Bayesian updating provides a disciplined framework for changing your mind in response to evidence.
takeaways: Start with your current belief and update as evidence arrives
Stronger evidence should produce larger updates
Good thinkers hold beliefs loosely and update continuously

faq.question: What prevents people from updating their beliefs?
faq.answer: Confirmation bias filters evidence to match existing beliefs. Identity attachment makes changing your mind feel like losing part of yourself. Sunk cost fallacy makes abandoning a position feel wasteful. Social pressure punishes those who appear inconsistent. All of these resist rational updating.

faq.question: How strong should your prior beliefs be?
faq.answer: Hold priors proportional to the evidence that formed them. Beliefs based on extensive personal experience or rigorous research should be strong. Beliefs based on hearsay or limited anecdotes should be weak and easily updated. Calibrate confidence to the quality of your evidence.
